title: The Best Sniper Ever
dateline: The research base. A year later.
mood: Behind a wall of crates marked NO SIS, Chang’e builds Lesley a birthday present all by herself.

hero.alt: Chang'e works alone at a cluttered lab bench with her tongue between her teeth, a tool in her hand, the parts of a long red and gold rifle laid out before her, robot arms overhead and Mr. Bunny peeking up behind the bench.

segs.t: Lesley took her supper standing up, at the door of the small room where the family ate. From there she could watch the corridor and the table both.
That evening Chang’e’s mother set out a fourth plate.
Lesley counted them. Four. There had been four at the house.
“That one’s yours,” said Chang’e. She pulled out the chair. It faced the door. “Sit.”
Lesley sat.
Nobody said anything about it. Chang’e’s father ate in silence, as he always did. Over the soup he put down his spoon.
“How much can a soldier carry?” he asked. A while later he added, “And still run.”
“Thirty kilos,” said Lesley. “Twenty, if she has to run far.”
He wrote it on his napkin.
“Dad,” said Chang’e. “No work at dinner.”
He folded the napkin into his pocket anyway.
A few days later a researcher found Chang’e at the big bench, standing on a box to reach it.
“That bench is for grown-ups,” he said. “Back to your corner.”
Chang’e did not get off the box. “I’m telling Big Sis on you!”
He laughed. “Who?”
Then he turned around. Lesley stood in the doorway. She had not said anything. She did not say anything now.
He remembered some work at the far end of the lab.
Nobody had called her that in front of people before. Lesley did not correct it. She looked at the box under the small boots.
I had a crate,
she thought.
That night her round found the lab light still on. Chang’e was asleep at the big bench, her cheek on the wood, the soldering iron still in her hand.
Lesley took the iron out of her fingers, set it in its stand and switched it off. Then she lifted her. The child weighed less than twenty kilos. Lesley could have run with her.
“I’m not asleep,” said Chang’e into her shoulder. “I’m thinking with my eyes shut.”
“Think in bed.”
Mr. Bunny followed them down the corridor, yawning on his screen.
Later that week Chang’e had a sore throat, and it made her furious. Her mother put one pill on the bench, beside a cup of water.
“No,” croaked Chang’e.
Her mother did not argue. She took her mug of tea to the doorway and leaned there, sipping.
Lesley was checking the window locks. She checked them slowly.
The mug emptied. The pill was gone.
On her way out, Chang’e’s mother spoke to Lesley without stopping. “Never argue with her. She enjoys it.”
Lesley memorized that, the way she memorized a sight line.
Every morning she signed the gate log with the date. This year she knew which date was hers. It was two weeks off.
Last year was enough,
she thought. She told nobody the date.
At dusk Chang’e crossed the yard in her child-sized lab coat, with an armful of springs from the stores. Mr. Bunny floated at her shoulder.

The blonde girl was at the outer fence again. She was older than Chang’e, and she came most evenings to watch the base’s machines through the wire. Chang’e shifted the springs to one arm and waved. The girl did not wave back.
At the back of the lab stood the test ring, a steel hoop taller than her father. Its jointed arms could hold work up in the air.
Weeks ago Chang’e had shoved crates into a wall around it, one shoulder at a time. Every crate was taller than she was. Mr. Bunny had pushed from the other side. It did nothing, but he liked to help.
A sign on the crates said NO SIS.
Inside the wall, she set down the springs and turned her design log back to its first page.

media.alt: Chang'e carries a box of parts and tools across the bright lab, frowning with effort, while Mr. Bunny hovers behind her and an open notebook lies on the bench in front.

segs.t: It had started with a night at the lab window. The Shield had called Sis out to the city’s edge, and Chang’e watched the gate until dawn. Sis came back with mud to her knees. The tape on her old Shield rifle’s stock hung in strips.
If she can hit them from farther away,
Chang’e had thought,
they can’t reach her.
But Sis handed things back. The lamp. The gloves.
Not regulation.
So Chang’e had borrowed the Shield’s rulebook from the gate office and read it cover to cover. A Shield rifle, the book said, was worked by hand and needed nothing else.
Regulation, then,
she had thought.
Nothing she can hand back.
Her mother began every project with who it was for. So at the top of the first page Chang’e had written:
Lesley, my dear, dear protector, I want to make her the best sniper ever!
From that page on, she wrote every entry in that log to Lesley.
This one she was building alone. Last year her father’s hands had set the smallest parts of the eye. This time every part would be hers.

The barrel was longer than she was tall. She could not lift it, so the ring’s arms held it up for her. She soldered with her tongue between her teeth, while Mr. Bunny fetched whatever she pointed at. Then she filed the bolt until it ran smooth, and filed it again.
The night before the birthday, Lesley’s footsteps came down the lab at midnight. They passed the crates and did not stop. Sis obeyed signs.
Chang’e tightened the last screw. She stepped back.
“Phew, all done.”
She lay down on the floor under the ring and looked up at what hung in it. Mr. Bunny settled against her shoulder and looked too.
On the birthday, Lesley signed the gate log at dawn. Her pen stopped on the date. Then it went on.
Nobody mentioned it all day. Lesley had expected that. It was correct.
At dusk she came off the gate. A small hand took hold of her coat sleeve.
“Your shift ended four minutes ago,” said Chang’e. “I checked.”
She walked ahead through the lab and did not let go. The two Doctors sat at their bench with their backs to the room. They did not turn around. Their hands lay still on the bench.
Chang’e tore the sign off the crates and dragged one aside. Behind it stood the ring. A rifle hung in its jointed arms, red and gold, longer than Chang’e was tall.
“Ta-da! Now you’ll be the BEST sniper ever!” said Chang’e, and she spread both arms toward the ring.

media.alt: In a bright lab a red and gold rifle hangs in the jointed arms of a tall steel ring, and small Chang'e flings both arms out toward it; then Lesley, her gold hair over one eye, stares at it without a word.

segs.t: The ring’s arms opened and let the rifle down into Lesley’s hands.
It was heavy in the right places. Lesley worked the bolt. It slid like a door on good hinges and locked home. Clack.
There was no cell in it and no cable. A spring, a pin and a bolt. Her hand cocked it, and her finger fired it.
Her father’s bench had sounded like that, with every clock on the wall going. The night the roof came down, every lamp in the house had died. The clocks he wound by hand kept ticking.
It’ll still work in the dark,
she thought.
Lesley held the rifle and did not move.
Chang’e’s arms had come down. She was watching Lesley’s hands, the way she had watched them over the lamp and the gloves.
“It’s regulation,” she said quickly. “I read the whole book. Twice.”
Lesley did not hand it back.
“Now you can’t miss,” said Chang’e.
Lesley looked down the length of the barrel, then at her. “I always hit my target.”
Chang’e stared at her. Then she laughed so hard she sat down on the floor. Mr. Bunny’s screen laughed with her. At their bench, both her parents looked up.
She’s laughing at something I said,
Lesley thought.
Lesley crouched. Her free hand came up, and this time it did not stop halfway. It settled on the small head and stayed there a moment.
Then she carried the rifle to the far wall and put it to her shoulder. She sighted down the lab on the clock over the door, with both eyes open, the real one and the teal one.
She worked the bolt. Clack.
